# Comparing Two Groups {#sec-comparing-groups}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Sample chapter

This short sample shows the structure every chapter will follow. In the full book, this material belongs to Chapter 6.
:::



## Elaf's question

Half of the 600 students in Elaf's study were invited, at random, to a six-week wellbeing workshop after their first semester. At the end of semester 2, Elaf wants to know:

> **Did the workshop improve students' wellbeing?**

The invited students' average wellbeing is higher than the others'. But averages always differ a little between any two groups, even when nothing real is going on. The question is whether the difference is bigger than chance alone would produce. A **t-test** answers exactly that question.

## The idea on a handful of numbers

Imagine only five students in each group, with these wellbeing scores (out of 100):


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
invited     <- c(68, 72, 65, 75, 70)
not_invited <- c(62, 66, 60, 69, 64)

mean(invited)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 70
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
mean(not_invited)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 64.2
```


:::
:::


The invited group is 5.8 points higher on average. Is that more than chance? `t.test()` compares the two groups:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
small_test <- t.test(invited, not_invited)
small_test
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

	Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  invited and not_invited
t = 2.5099, df = 7.9411, p-value = 0.03658
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
  0.4642934 11.1357066
sample estimates:
mean of x mean of y 
     70.0      64.2 
```


:::
:::


The important number is the **p-value**. It tells you how often a difference at least this large would appear by chance alone, if the workshop had no effect at all. Here it is 0.037: a difference this large would happen by chance about 4 times in 100. By convention, researchers call a result **statistically significant** when the p-value is below 0.05.

## Elaf's data

Now the same test on the real study. First, combine each student's workshop group (in `students`) with their semester 2 wellbeing score (in `semesters`):


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
semester2 <- merge(students, semesters[semesters$semester == 2, ],
                   by = "student_id")
nrow(semester2)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 600
```


:::
:::


Always look at the data before testing it. @fig-workshop shows wellbeing in each group.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(semester2, aes(x = workshop, y = wellbeing, fill = workshop)) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE, width = 0.5) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Wellbeing (0 to 100)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Wellbeing at the end of semester 2, by workshop group. Each box shows the middle half of the students; the line inside is the median.](comparing-groups_files/figure-html/fig-workshop-1.png){#fig-workshop fig-alt='Box plot of wellbeing scores for invited and not-invited students. The invited group\'s box sits a few points higher.' width=576}
:::
:::


The invited group sits a little higher, but the two groups overlap a lot. Now the test:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
result <- t.test(wellbeing ~ workshop, data = semester2)
result
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

	Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  wellbeing by workshop
t = 5.469, df = 597.52, p-value = 6.66e-08
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group Invited and group Not invited is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 3.364699 7.135301
sample estimates:
    mean in group Invited mean in group Not invited 
                    65.47                     60.22 
```


:::
:::




Invited students scored 5.2 points higher on average (65.5 against 60.2), and the p-value is below 0.001. A difference this large would almost never appear by chance, so Elaf can conclude that the workshop improved wellbeing. Because students were invited **at random**, she can say the workshop *caused* the improvement, not just that it went with it.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Writing it up in a thesis

"Students invited to the wellbeing workshop reported higher wellbeing at the end of semester 2 (M = 65.5) than those not invited (M = 60.2), a difference of 5.2 points, *t*(598) = 5.47, *p* < .001."
:::

Notice that the numbers in that sentence are not typed in: they come from the code. If the data changed, the text would update itself.

## Which test when?

The t-test is one of several tests for comparing groups. The diagram shows where it fits. Chapter 6 covers each of these.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
  A[What are you comparing?] --> B{How many groups?}
  B -->|Two| C{Same people measured twice?}
  B -->|Three or more| F[ANOVA]
  C -->|No, different people| D[Two-sample t-test]
  C -->|Yes| E[Paired t-test]
  D -.->|Data very skewed| G[Mann-Whitney U test]
  E -.->|Data very skewed| H[Wilcoxon signed-rank test]
```

::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## In your field: health research

The t-test was invented to analyse small medical experiments [@student1908]. R still includes one of the original datasets, `sleep`: the extra hours of sleep that 10 patients gained with each of two sleeping drugs. Because the *same* patients took both drugs, this calls for a **paired** t-test:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
drug1 <- sleep$extra[sleep$group == 1]
drug2 <- sleep$extra[sleep$group == 2]
t.test(drug2, drug1, paired = TRUE)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

	Paired t-test

data:  drug2 and drug1
t = 4.0621, df = 9, p-value = 0.002833
alternative hypothesis: true mean difference is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.7001142 2.4598858
sample estimates:
mean difference 
           1.58 
```


:::
:::


Patients slept on average 1.6 hours longer with the second drug.
:::

## Chapter review

**Summary**

- Two group averages almost always differ a little. A t-test asks whether the difference is larger than chance would produce.
- The p-value is how often a difference at least this large would appear by chance if there were no real effect. Below 0.05 is usually called statistically significant.
- Always plot the groups before testing them.
- Random assignment, as in Elaf's workshop, lets you draw causal conclusions.

**Key terms**: t-test, p-value, statistically significant, paired t-test, random assignment.

**Practise**: the exercises for this chapter will be in the [playground](../playground/index.html).
